<header class="dg-head dg-head-section"><p class="dg-kicker">Appendix B <span class="dg-sep">•</span> <a href="index.html">Proofs &amp; Comments</a></p><h1 class="dg-title"><span class="dg-secnum">B.5</span> Chart-induced basis of <span class="math inline">\(T_p\mathcal{M}\)</span> (§<a class="dg-xref" href="../tangent-spaces/tangent-space.html#subsection_Basis_and_Coordinate_Components_of_TpM" data-kind="subsection" data-label="subsection_Basis_and_Coordinate_Components_of_TpM">4.1.1</a>)</h1></header>
<p>In this appendix, we provide a formal proof that the set of chart-induced vectors <span class="math display">\[
    \left\lbrace \left( \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{X}^1} \right)_p,\; \ldots,\; \left( \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{X}^d} \right)_p \right\rbrace
\]</span> constitutes a basis for the tangent space <span class="math inline">\(T_p\mathcal{M}\)</span> at a point <span class="math inline">\(p \in \mathcal{M}\)</span>, associated with a given chart <span class="math inline">\((\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X})\)</span> containing <span class="math inline">\(p\)</span>. While this fact is often presented as an immediate consequence of definitions, it is instructive—and mathematically rigorous—to explicitly verify that these elements indeed satisfy the conditions of a basis:</p>
<ul class="dg-itemize dg-depth-1">
<li><p><strong>Spanning:</strong>  Any <span class="math inline">\(v_{\gamma, p} \in T_p\mathcal{M}\)</span> can be written as a linear combination of the basis elements in <span class="math inline">\(e\)</span>. This condition holds immediately from the expression given in Section <a class="dg-xref" href="../tangent-spaces/tangent-space.html#subsection_Basis_and_Coordinate_Components_of_TpM" data-kind="subsection" data-label="subsection_Basis_and_Coordinate_Components_of_TpM">4.1.1</a>:  <span class="math display">\begin{align*}
            v_{\gamma, p} = \sum_{i=1}^{d} \dot{\gamma}^i_{\mathcal{U}}(\lambda_0)
            \cdot \left( \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{X}^i} \right)_{p}
        \end{align*}</span>  Here we show that any tangent vector <span class="math inline">\(v_{\gamma, p}\)</span> can be represented in a chart <span class="math inline">\(\left(\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X}\right)\)</span> as the linear combination of the basis elements <span class="math inline">\(\left( \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{X}^i} \right)_{p}\)</span>.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>Linear independence:</strong> The only linear combination of basis elements that yields the zero vector in <span class="math inline">\(T_p\mathcal{M}\)</span> is the trivial one where all coefficients vanish. To see this, suppose that some linear combination of the basis elements gives the zero vector:  <span class="math display">\begin{align*}
            0 = \sum_{i=1}^d \alpha^i \cdot \left( \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{X}^i} \right)_{p}.
        \end{align*}</span>  Our goal here is to check if this condition holds only when all the coefficients <span class="math inline">\(\alpha^i\)</span> are zero independently (if so, we will have proven linear independence), or if there exists other possible combinations of the coefficients <span class="math inline">\(\alpha^i\)</span> that also yield the zero vector as a result.</p>
<div class="dg-skip dg-medskip"></div>
<p>If we now let this expression (both sides) act upon any arbitrary basis element <span class="math inline">\(\mathscr{X}^j\)</span>:  <span class="math display">\begin{align*}
            0 =
            \sum_{i=1}^d \alpha^i \cdot \left( \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{X}^i} \right)_{p}
            (\mathscr{X}^j).
        \end{align*}</span>  At this point we need to realize that, by definition (see Section <a class="dg-xref" href="../tangent-spaces/tangent-space.html#subsection_Basis_and_Coordinate_Components_of_TpM" data-kind="subsection" data-label="subsection_Basis_and_Coordinate_Components_of_TpM">4.1.1</a>):  <span class="math display">\begin{align*}
            \left( \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{X}^i} \right)_{p} (\mathscr{X}^j) =
            \partial_i \underbrace{\left[ \mathscr{X}^j \circ \mathscr{X}^{-1}\right]}_{\mathbb{R} \longleftarrow \mathbb{R}^d} (\mathscr{X}(p)) =
            \delta^j_i.
        \end{align*}</span></p>
<p>This is a direct consequence of the fact that the operator <span class="math inline">\(\left( \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{X}^i} \right)_p\)</span> measures the rate of change of any function along the <span class="math inline">\(i\)</span>-th coordinate direction at the point <span class="math inline">\(p\)</span>. When applied to the coordinate function <span class="math inline">\(\mathscr{X}^j\)</span>, which simply “extracts” the <span class="math inline">\(j\)</span>-th coordinate, it yields <span class="math inline">\(1\)</span> if it differentiates with respect to its own direction (<span class="math inline">\(i = j\)</span>), and <span class="math inline">\(0\)</span> otherwise.</p>
<div class="dg-skip dg-medskip"></div>
<p>Substituting everything on our original expression we have:  <span class="math display">\begin{align*}
            0 =
            \sum_{i=1}^d \alpha^i \cdot \left( \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{X}^i} \right)_{p}
            (\mathscr{X}^j).
            \;\iff\;
            0 = \sum_{i=1}^d \alpha^i \cdot \delta^j_i = \alpha^j
            \quad \forall j=1,\dots,d.
        \end{align*}</span>  The conclusion <span class="math inline">\(\alpha^j = 0\)</span> for all <span class="math inline">\(j\)</span> follows immediately because we have let the original expression act upon any arbitrary basis element <span class="math inline">\(\mathscr{X}^j\)</span>. Therefore, the assumption that the linear combination vanishes implies that each individual coefficient must be zero independently. This guarantees that no non-trivial linear dependence exists among the basis elements, completing the proof of linear independence.</p></li>
</ul>
